questions.prompt: In a source follower, which capacitance is Miller-transformed and why?
options: \(C_{gd}\), because the drain is the output
\(C_{db}\), because it is largest
\(C_{gs}\), because it connects the input (gate) to the output (source)
None; followers have no bridging capacitor
questions.explanation: The drain is at AC ground, so \(C_{gd}\) simply loads the gate; \(C_{gs}\) bridges gate and source (reader Sec. 14.8.1).

questions.prompt: What does it mean that \(C_{gs}\) is bootstrapped in a follower?
options: It is charged once at power-up and stays charged
It is shorted by the bias network
It is multiplied by the gain
Both of its terminals move almost together, so almost no current flows through it
questions.explanation: The gain across it is nearly \(+1\), so the voltage across it hardly changes.

questions.prompt: Now the follower drives a resistive load so that \(g_mR_L' = 4\). With \(C_{gd} = 5\ \mathrm{fF}\) and \(C_{gs} = 30\ \mathrm{fF}\), find the input capacitance in fF.
questions.explanation: \(A_v = 4/5 = 0.8\), so \(C_{in} = 5 + 0.2\times30 = 11\ \mathrm{fF}\). A heavier load weakens the bootstrapping.

questions.prompt: Driven from a large \(R_s\), a follower's output impedance rises with frequency. Why can that cause ringing with a capacitive load?
options: A rising output impedance looks inductive, and with \(C_L\) it forms a resonant pair
Because \(g_m\) rises with frequency
Because \(C_{gd}\) becomes negative
Followers cannot ring; their gain is below one
questions.explanation: At low frequency \(Z_{out} \approx 1/g_m\); as \(C_{gs}\) shorts out, \(Z_{out}\) climbs toward \(R_s\), an inductive-looking rise.

questions.prompt: Preview of big circuits: when hunting for the dominant pole, how should you treat a follower's output node?
options: As the dominant pole by default
As a low-impedance node (about \(1/g_m\)), usually not the dominant pole
As an open circuit
As a high-impedance node
questions.explanation: Dominant poles live at high-impedance nodes; followers create low-impedance ones.

questions.prompt: Preview of big circuits: why might a designer insert a follower between two gain stages?
options: To add voltage gain
To reduce power
To isolate a high-impedance node from a large or Miller-multiplied capacitance
To remove the need for biasing
questions.explanation: The follower's low output resistance drives the capacitance instead of the high-impedance node.
questions.figure_alt: CS cascade with an internal source-follower buffer: node 1 (C_M1) at the input; node 2 with R_o1 and only C_db1 + C_gd2 (C_2); the follower (gain about 1) drives node 3 whose resistance is only 1/g_m2, loaded by the next stage's Miller capacitance C_M3; the last stage drives R_o3 and C_db.
